scope: Missing garment-strike pickets and union defendants: actual multi-day custody, distinct bail-separated detention segments, eight identified archival portraits. Existing records preserved wholesale.

nyt-release.label: New York Times, December 21, 1909, p.1, Autos For Strikers In Shirtwaist War; primary transcription in Alexander Street Documents. Bertha Eltren released the previous day after five-day workhouse commitment.

call-release.label: New York Call, December 21, 1909, p.1, Rousing Welcome Given to Girls Released From Workhouse. Original scan spells her name Bertha Elkins and reports release yesterday morning.

ilgwu5.label: ILGWU News-History (1950), chapter 5, pp.1, 3-4; reprints Josephine Casey letter from Kalamazoo County Jail, Detroit Times May 4, 1912, and identified 1912 cell photograph.

casey-bio.label: Delia Tash, Penn State librarian, Biographical Sketch of Josephine Casey, Alexander Street; 1950 death year. Birth year conflicts with other biographical sources and is withheld.

cornell-trial.label: Cornell Kheel Center, court collection 6036/011, Guide to the Sigman, Morris (Max) Trial, Criminal Case: individual arrests, releases on bail, remand, dismissal and trial outcomes.

july-letter.label: The Ladies Garment Worker, July 1915, printed p.3 / scan p.7: message from the Tombs signed by all eight jailed defendants, including Louis Holzer.

ilgwu6.label: ILGWU News-History (1950), chapter 6, pp.1, 4: reprints October 9, 1915 New York Call acquittal report and The World trial photograph with seven individual identifications.

sigman-bio.label: Cornell Kheel Center ILGWU Presidents: Morris Sigman, birth 1880, death 1931 and union leadership history.

casey-later.label: Josephine Casey to Samuel Gompers, April 30, 1914, New York; Samuel Gompers Papers, University of Maryland. Her signed account of organizing and travel after the 1912 jail episode confirms subsequent freedom, without fixing a release date.

prisoner.name: Bertha Elkins
prisoner.description: Bertha Elkins was a picket in the 1909 New York shirtwaist strike. Contemporary newspapers describe her release from the Blackwell’s Island workhouse and the reception organized by fellow strikers and the Women’s Trade Union League.

cases.charges: Strike-picketing prosecution; individual statutory charge unverified
cases.sentence: Sent to the Blackwell’s Island workhouse for five days by Magistrate Barlow. The December 21, 1909 newspapers report her release the previous morning, December 20. The exact arrest and commitment days are not established; no start date is calculated by subtracting the sentence.

case_research.custody_evidence: Two contemporary release reports establish completed multi-day workhouse custody, not simply an arrest or a sentence that might have been suspended.

entries.custody_evidence: Two contemporary release reports establish completed multi-day workhouse custody, not simply an arrest or a sentence that might have been suspended.
entries.status_research: Historical custody verified. Existing profiles, cases and photos are preserved. No unsupported vital dates, coordinates, current incarceration, institutional relation or personal support website inferred. The Call prints Bertha Elkins; the Times transcription uses Bertha Eltren for the matching December 20 release and WTUL reception. Both spellings are screened as one identity. Age 19 is not converted to an exact birthdate. Participation in the Local 25-led strike does not establish formal Local 25 membership; only the strike affiliation is assigned.

prisoner.name: Josephine Casey
prisoner.description: Josephine Casey was a labor organizer who helped lead the 1912 Kalamazoo corset workers’ strike over wages and factory conditions. She was jailed during the campaign and wrote from Kalamazoo County Jail about the workers’ demands.

cases.charges: Contempt of court for defying the injunction against Kalamazoo corset strike picketing
cases.sentence: The Detroit Times published her letter from Kalamazoo County Jail on May 4, 1912. She reported having spent nearly a week in jail. The exact commitment day, full individual sentence and release date are not established by that letter. Its publication date is not entered as the date custody began.

case_research.custody_evidence: Casey’s signed jail letter expressly describes nearly a week of actual confinement; the union’s reproduced contemporary report identifies the strike injunction and contempt proceeding.

entries.custody_evidence: Casey’s signed jail letter expressly describes nearly a week of actual confinement; the union’s reproduced contemporary report identifies the strike injunction and contempt proceeding.
entries.status_research: Historical custody verified. Existing profiles, cases and photos are preserved. No unsupported vital dates, coordinates, current incarceration, institutional relation or personal support website inferred. Secondary accounts report 37 days, but the verified primary letter establishes only nearly a week as of publication. Do not convert 37 days into exact endpoints. Birth 1876 in the suffrage sketch conflicts with 1878? in other biographies; no birthday or birth year entered. Death 1950 is documented; exact day withheld pending stronger verification. No current-custody flag, and later release is not dated. Her April 30, 1914 letter from New York describes her later organizing and travel; this establishes subsequent release, but does not supply its exact date. The release-status flag is true; the release-date field remains empty.

photo.identity_evidence: Printed caption expressly identifies Josephine Casey as the seated woman and Belle Yount as the standing woman in the Kalamazoo cell.

prisoner.name: Morris Sigman
prisoner.description: Morris Sigman was an International Ladies Garment Workers Union union secretary-treasurer detained in the prosecution arising from Herman Liebowitz’s death during the 1910 New York cloakmakers’ strike. He was acquitted at the end of the trial. He later served as ILGWU president from 1923 to 1928.

cases.charges: Murder accusation connected to the 1910 cloakmakers strike; preliminary 1914 detention
cases.sentence: Arrested and held without bail in April 1914, then released on bail before the union convention. The prosecution remained pending, with repeated adjournments. The exact bail-release day is not established. This initial custody is separate from the later 1915 recommitments; no conviction or prison sentence resulted.

cases.charges: Murder accusation connected to the 1910 cloakmakers strike; May 1915 pretrial detention
cases.sentence: Arrested May 11, 1915 and detained without bail. A July 1915 message from the Tombs bears his name. Bail was set on August 7; the actual day he left jail is unverified and is not equated with the bail-order date. The later September 19 return to jail establishes an intervening release. This is the first 1915 custody segment, not continuous detention through trial.

cases.charges: First-degree murder charge; acquitted
cases.sentence: Returned to jail September 19, 1915 for the first-degree murder trial, which began September 23. The jury acquitted him October 8, 1915. Contemporary reporting describes the five acquitted defendants leaving for home that evening. No prison sentence was imposed. This is the separate trial-custody segment after the earlier release on bail.

case_research.custody_evidence: Cornell’s court-collection narrative documents the named April arrest, detention without bail and subsequent release before the union convention.
The May arrest and the individually signed July message from jail establish sustained confinement. Subsequent bail proceedings and case disposition establish that this historical custody ended.
Cornell documents September 19 remand; the contemporary October 9 report supplies the separate Thursday dismissal and Friday acquittal outcomes. Trial custody lasted more than two weeks.
